content:
Lets say we define an Atom to be an unordered pair of Terms (to represent an equation of terms).
I want to write (and verify) an executable unification algorithm that takes as input an Atom.
If the both sides of the Atom are variables the algorithm needs to make a choice which one to assign to the other one, so it won't be well defined on Atoms.
However the property that i care about - that the output of the function is some unifier for the atom -
is symmetric/independent of the order of the input pair.
So if i only knew this fact about the function and wouldn't be able to look at the exact output value that would in some sense be well defined again.
I presume there isn't, but is there any way to use the underlying sorted pair of the Atom for such a function in Lean (keeping it executable)?
It's a bit difficult to tell without an #mwe, but perhaps you're looking for docs#Quot.unqot

Indeed there's two options for getting an element underlying the quotient: there is docs#Quot.unquot which is unsafe but computable (returns the actual code representation, which means it is not well-defined as a function, so it is unsafe), and there is docs#Quot.out which is sound but non-computable (it uses choice to choose a canonical representation for each equivalence class)
Other than that, if you want something you can prove things about, the best options are docs#Sym2.rec and similar (e.g. Sym2.recOn, Sym2.ind, etc)

I'm not sure what you're asking but something you can do is to have the function take in ordered pairs of terms, and then have the property be about the function and an unordered pair of terms, if it really is a symmetric property.

Aaron Liu schrieb:

I'm not sure what you're asking but something you can do is to have the function take in ordered pairs of terms, and then have the property be about the function and an unordered pair of terms, if it really is a symmetric property.

But i want to actually run the function on an explicit unordered pair at some point and i can't input that
You can only use an unordered pair of the result doesn't depend on which order the pair is in
so if your function does depend on the order you will have to continue processing its output until you get something that doesn't depend on the order
or you can also just do a Quot.unquot and be unsound if you don't care about proving stuff about it
Yea, i think there is just no way to do what i want
I still don't know what you want

Lets say f : Sym2 (Term) -> Unifier, so f takes as input an unordered pair s(t1, t2) and outputs a unifier of s(t1, t2) (lets ignore that this doesn't always exist, so one has to return an Option...). For the case where t1 = var x1 and t2 = var x2 it needs to choose for the output unifier wether to assign x1 ↦ x2 or x2 ↦ x1. In full abstraction there is no way to choose, so we want to use the axiom of choice for this.
One can then prove the (only) important property i care about, namely that the output will always be a unifier of s(t1, t2) regardless of the choice taken. But choice will make the function noncomputable though and i really want to execute it.

I wonder why we can't use the mechanism that Quot.unquot uses to make such a function computable.
This should in principle be "okay" (whatever that exactly means), since one cannot ever know which choice was given to us in the definition - so any choice (in particular the VM choice) should be okay

The problem is that the behavior of Quot.unquot is observable (through #eval / native_decide). Even if you decide not to care about native_decide, what you end up with is a function that doesn't behave like specified; so if you write some proof about your function, then it might not hold for the actual implementation.
One thing you could do is make the output Squash too, i.e. provide a function (x : Sym2 Term) -> Squash (Unifier x) (or Trunc? I don't think we've decided how to handle this duplication yet)

Robin Arnez schrieb:

One thing you could do is make the output Squash too, i.e. provide a function (x : Sym2 Term) -> Squash (Unifier x) (or Trunc? I don't think we've decided how to handle this duplication yet)

From looking at it, this requires me to

  1. Rewrite the rest of any program using the Unifier as a function in the unifier
  2. Prove that the output of the program is the same for any choice of unifier
    which is very impractical

Robin Arnez schrieb:

The problem is that the behavior of Quot.unquot is observable (through #eval / native_decide). Even if you decide not to care about native_decide, what you end up with is a function that doesn't behave like specified; so if you write some proof about your function, then it might not hold for the actual implementation.

I'm not familiar with #eval and native_decide - are you saying they can be used to (in a proof) determine what the output of Quot.out is? Can you break down the problem a bit further for me?

Let me make an example:

def test (x : Squash Nat) : Nat := unsafe unsafeCast x

theorem test_one_eq_test_two : test (Squash.mk 1) = test (Squash.mk 2) := by
  congr 1; apply Subsingleton.allEq

#guard test (Squash.mk 1) = 1
#guard test (Squash.mk 2) = 2
#guard test (Squash.mk 1) ≠ test (Squash.mk 2)

As you can see from this example (Quot.unquot is just unsafeCast btw), at runtime, test (Squash.mk n) simply returns n so for example test (Squash.mk 1) = 1 and test (Squash.mk 2) = 2 (at runtime). However, because Squash (i.e. the quotient by the always true relation) is a subsingleton, both should return the same value because of congruence. So the runtime behavior here diverges from the model.
Specifically, the problem is that Quot.unquot is not a choice function but a function that breaks congruence.
I think i understand now, thanks!

Robin Arnez ha dicho:

I made a recent Lean core PR which makes Squash and Trunc identical in implementation. The idea is to deprecate Trunc in favor of Squash but I haven't found the time to make that PR. Help welcome!
